objectives.objective: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
keyPoints: Move knowledge and policy out of developers' heads into version-controlled artifacts the tool reads: CLAUDE.md for conventions, committed project settings.json for shared policy, user settings for personal preferences.
Deterministic vs probabilistic: memory files and prompts raise likelihood; hooks and permission allow/deny rules execute every time.
Must-happen behaviours (lint before finishing, never read .env, no destructive commands without approval) belong in hooks and permission rules.
Keep CLAUDE.md lean — it consumes context every session; stable conventions belong there, live external data behind MCP servers.
Deny rules for secrets paths belong in shared settings from day one.
objectives.watchFor: Documenting standards in a wiki codifies drift rather than eliminating it, because nothing enforces what the wiki says — and per-developer permission settings make security depend on whose laptop is open.

question.stem: A team requires that the linter run after every file edit, without exception. Where should this be configured?
options: A hook in the committed project settings that runs after edit operations
An instruction in the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude to lint after editing
A team wiki page describing the linting standard
A custom slash command developers invoke when they finish editing
question.answerWhy: A behaviour that must happen every time needs deterministic execution, and a hook in shared committed settings runs regardless of what the model decides. A CLAUDE.md instruction is probabilistic, a wiki enforces nothing, and a slash command depends on someone remembering to invoke it.

objectives.objective: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
keyPoints: Workflow-first adoption: start from the delivery constraint — review latency, test debt, slow onboarding, doc rot — and apply tooling where it relieves the bottleneck.
Theory of constraints applies: accelerating code generation when review is the bottleneck just deepens the review queue.
High-value applications: AI-assisted first-pass review, test generation against untested code, refactoring support, documentation, and navigating unfamiliar codebases.
Measure delivery outcomes — cycle time, PR throughput, change-failure rate, developer satisfaction — against a baseline captured before rollout.
Managed rollout: pilot with a real team on real backlog work, publish guidelines, measure for a defined period, expand on evidence.
objectives.watchFor: Adoption percentage, AI-generated lines of code, and acceptance rate are vanity metrics — they can all rise while the organization ships no faster. A named human stays accountable for merged code.

question.stem: A team's delivery bottleneck is code review latency. Leadership proposes rolling out AI code generation and reporting adoption percentage as the success metric. What should the architect recommend?
options: Proceed as proposed, since faster code generation increases overall throughput
Target the review bottleneck with AI-assisted first-pass review, and measure cycle time and PR throughput against a pre-rollout baseline
Roll out generation first and address review capacity in a later phase
Add reviewers rather than tooling, since the constraint is human capacity
question.answerWhy: Accelerating a non-bottleneck step deepens the queue at the constraint, so the tooling should target review itself, measured by delivery outcomes against a baseline. Adoption percentage measures activity rather than throughput, deferring the constraint to a later phase guarantees the interim gets worse, and hiring alone forgoes the tooling leverage available at the bottleneck.

objectives.objective: Support debugging and operational issue resolution
keyPoints: Split permissions on the observe/act boundary: read-only access to logs, metrics, traces, and code for diagnosis; explicit human approval for any state-changing action.
Mid-incident is when supervision is least reliable, which is exactly why the write path needs a deterministic gate.
A coherent explanation is not evidence — reproduce the failure with a test, confirm the patch makes it pass, and run the existing suite.
Learn the guessing signature: serially revised, authoritative root causes with shifting citations and no confirmed checks.
When that pattern appears, stop the AI-led thread and escalate to humans, handing over the hypotheses already eliminated.
objectives.watchFor: Restricting AI diagnosis to staging discards the live logs and state the investigation needs — read-only production access is the safe alternative, not a staging-only rule.

question.stem: During an outage, an assistant proposes a root cause and a config change with a clear, convincing explanation. What should happen before it is applied?
options: Apply it immediately — incident duration is the dominant cost
Reproduce the failure with a test, confirm the patch makes that test pass, and run the existing suite
Ask the assistant to rate its confidence in the diagnosis and apply it if confidence is high
Have a second model review the proposed change before applying it
question.answerWhy: Fluency is not evidence, so the fix must be verified against the system's actual behaviour via a reproducing test plus the existing suite. Applying immediately risks turning one outage into two, self-rated confidence structures the guess without adding ground truth, and a second model is another probabilistic opinion rather than a check against reality.
